'''Nick Montfort''' is an American computer scientist and poet who is a professor of [[digital media]] at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], where he directs a lab called The Trope Tank.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Electronic literature|last=Rettberg, Scott|isbn=978-1-5095-1677-3|location=Cambridge, UK|oclc=1028213515|date = 2019-01-09}}</ref> He also holds a part-time position at the [[University of Bergen]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nick Montfort, MIT Professor of Digital Media, Appointed Professor II at UiB Digital Culture |url=https://www.uib.no/en/discipline/digitalculture/128711/nick-montfort-mit-professor-digital-media-appointed-professor-ii |access-date=2022-10-12 |website=University of Bergen |language=en}}</ref> where he leads a node on computational narrative systems at the Center for Digital Narrative.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Partners and people at the Center for Digital Narrative |url=https://www.uib.no/en/cdn/138238/partners-and-people |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220923213443/https://www.uib.no/en/cdn/138238/partners-and-people |url-status=dead |archive-date=September 23, 2022 |access-date=2022-10-12 |website=University of Bergen |language=en}}</ref> Among his publications are seven books of [[Natural-language generation|computer-generated literature]] and six books from the [[MIT Press]], several of which are collaborations. His work also includes digital projects, many of them in the form of short programs.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/nick-montfort|title=Nick Montfort|date=2019-11-26|website=Poetry Foundation|language=en|access-date=2019-11-26}}</ref> He lives in [[New York City]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.victoriaadvocate.com/calendar/nick-montfort-uhv-american-book-review-reading-series-speaker/event_2d13cfb0-db0a-11e9-9f10-03ad265f4c95.html|title=Nick Montfort, UHV American Book Review Reading Series Speaker|website=The Victoria Advocate|language=en|access-date=2019-11-26}}</ref>

== Computer-generated books ==
Montfort's ''The Truelist'' (Counterpath, 2017) is a computer-generated book-length poem produced by a one-page computer program. The code is included at the end of the book.<ref>{{Cite book|title=The artist in the machine : the world of AI powered creativity|last=Miller, Arthur I.|isbn=978-0-262-04285-7|location=Cambridge, Massachusetts|oclc=1080249147|date = October 2019}}</ref> Montfort has also done a complete studio recording reading ''The Truelist,'' available at [[PennSound]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://writing.upenn.edu/pennsound/x/Montfort.php|title=PennSound: Nick Montfort|website=writing.upenn.edu|access-date=2019-11-26}}</ref>

Among Montfort's computer-generated books is ''#!'' (pronounced "shebang"), in which he "chooses the programming languages [[Python (programming language)|Python]], [[Ruby (programming language)|Ruby]], and [[Perl]] (the last of which has [[Black Perl|a documented history]] as a poetic medium) to create impressions of an ideal—machines based on the rules of language."<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.foundpoetryreview.com/blog/book-review-nick-montfort/|title=Book Review: #! {{!}} The Found Poetry Review|website=www.foundpoetryreview.com|language=en-US|access-date=2018-07-21}}</ref> The book includes a Python version of "Taroko Gorge," which is available online in [[JavaScript]] and has been modified by many authors.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://iloveepoetry.com/?page_id=7907|title=Taroko Gorge and Its Remixes|date=2013-11-15|work=I ♥ E-Poetry|access-date=2018-07-21|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Marques da Silva|first1=Ana|last2=Bettencourt|first2=Sandra|date=2017-04-18|title=Writing–reading devices: intermediations|journal=Neohelicon|language=en|volume=44|issue=1|pages=41–54|doi=10.1007/s11059-017-0382-0|hdl=10316/108485 |s2cid=151394868|issn=0324-4652|hdl-access=free}}</ref> Some of these "remixes" are collected in ''The Electronic Literature Collection: Volume 3.''<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://collection.eliterature.org/3/collection-taroko.html|title=Electronic Literature Collection - Volume 3|website=collection.eliterature.org|language=en-GB|access-date=2018-07-21}}</ref>

Montfort collaborated with six others on ''2x6,'' a book published by Les Figues that includes six short programs and some of the short narrative poems these generate in English, Spanish, French, Polish, Japanese, and Russian. This project has also been exhibited and is available online on the Web. Montfort's ''Autopia,'' which assembles short sentences from the names of automobiles, is another project that also appears as a printed book (published by Troll Thread), a gallery installation, and a web page. These and other of his computer-generated books have been considered [[conceptual writing]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=BIBLIOGRAPHY OF CONCEPTUAL WRITING.|last=ZELTIL, YIGRU.|date=2017|publisher=LULU COM|isbn=978-1-365-72551-7|location=[Place of publication not identified]|oclc=990024566}}</ref>

Several of Montfort's printed computer-generated books were generated with programs he wrote during [[National Novel Generation Month]] (NaNoGenMo). These include three self-published books, ''Hard West Turn (2018 Edition), Megawatt,'' and ''World Clock'', written during the first NaNoGenMo in 2014.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theverge.com/2014/11/25/7276157/nanogenmo-robot-author-novel|title=The strange world of computer-generated novels|last=Dzieza|first=Josh|date=2014-11-25|website=The Verge|language=en|access-date=2019-11-26}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.wired.com/story/nanogenmo-ai-novels-gpt2/|title=Text-Savvy AI Is Here to Write Fiction|magazine=Wired|access-date=2019-11-26|language=en|issn=1059-1028}}</ref> Translations of two of these were published by presses in Europe: ''World Clock'' was published in Polish translation by ha!art, and Megawatt in German translation by Frohmann.

Montfort is the founder and series editor of ''Using Electricity'', a series of computer-generated books published by Counterpath.

In November 2019 Montfort announced "Nano-NaNoGenMo," calling for short computer programs within that year's National Novel Generation Month. His request was that people write programs of 256 characters or less to generate novels of 50,000 words or more. He contributed several such programs himself, as did several others.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Citation|title=GitHub - NaNoGenMo/2019: National Novel Generation Month, 2019 edition|date=2019-11-26|url=https://github.com/NaNoGenMo/2019|publisher=National Novel Generation Month|access-date=2019-11-26}}</ref>

== Poetry ==
Montfort's poetry, in addition to computer-generated books and projects, includes digital poems that are collaborations with others. He, [[Amaranth Borsuk]] and [[Jesper Juul (game researcher)|Jesper Juul]] wrote ''The Deletionist,'' a system for generating [[Erasure (artform)|erasure poetry]] from any page on the web. With [[Stephanie Strickland]] he wrote ''Sea and Spar Between,'' a generator of about 225 trillion stanzas arranged in a grid and combining language from Herman Melville's ''Moby Dick'' and Emily Dickinson's poems.<ref>{{Cite book|title=This is not a copy : writing at the iterative turn|last=Marczewska, Kaja|isbn=978-1-5013-3783-3|location=New York|oclc=987796925|date = 2018-02-22}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=Aesthetic animism : digital poetry's ontological implications|last=Johnston, David Jhave|isbn=978-0-262-33439-6|location=Cambridge, Massachusetts|oclc=951678436|year = 2016}}</ref> Montfort and William Gillespie wrote ''2002: A Palindrome Story'', a 2002-word narrative palindrome published in 2002 in print and on the web.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Word toys poetry and technics|last=Stefans, Brian Kim|date=2015|publisher=The University of Alabama Press|others=Project Muse., Project MUSE|isbn=978-0-8173-9122-5|location=Tuscaloosa|oclc=993608334}}</ref>

''Riddle & Bind'' (Spineless Books, 2010), Montfort's first book of poetry, is a collection of poems written under constraint and literary riddles.

== Interactive fiction ==
Montfort has written about [[interactive fiction]] and written several interactive fiction games. ''Book and Volume'' (2005) was a finalist in the 2007 Slamdance Guerilla Gamemaker Competition. However, after ''[[Super Columbine Massacre RPG!]]'', which had also been named a finalist, was excluded from the festival, Montfort withdrew from the competition in protest.

Released in 2000,<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nM8oDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA184|title=The Cambridge Companion to Postmodern American Fiction|last=Geyh|first=Paula|date=April 24, 2017|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|page=184|isbn=9781107103443}}</ref> ''Ad Verbum'' is a wordplay-based game in which the player has to figure out stylistic constraints in different locations and type certain commands in order to solve puzzles.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=D2e8x_0AwokC&pg=PA464|title=The Routledge Companion to Experimental Literature|last1=Bray|first1=Joe|last2=Gibbons|first2=Alison|last3=McHale|first3=Brian|date=July 26, 2012|publisher=[[Routledge]]|page=464|isbn=9781136301742}}</ref> It received the 2000 XYZZY Award for Best Puzzles.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Electronic Art and Animation Catalog|date=2001|publisher=[[Association for Computing Machinery]]|page=102}}</ref>

''Twisty Little Passages: An Approach to Interactive Fiction,'' a 2003 book, was described by [[Steve Meretzky]] as "a thoroughly researched history of interactive fiction, as well as a brilliant analysis of the genre."<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://mitpress.mit.edu/books/twisty-little-passages|title=Twisty Little Passages|website=The MIT Press|date=7 November 2003|publisher=MIT Press|isbn=9780262134361|language=en|access-date=2018-07-21}}</ref>
{{clear}}

== Writing on digital media ==
The group blog ''Grand Text Auto,'' active in the early 2000s, was one site where Montfort wrote with others about digital media. Montfort wrote ''Twisty Little Passages: An Approach to [[Interactive Fiction]]'' (MIT Press, 2003) and co-edited ''The Electronic Literature Collection: Volume 1'' (ELO, 2006) and ''The New Media Reader'' (MIT Press, 2003)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/nick-montfort|title=Nick Montfort|date=2018-07-21|website=Poetry Foundation|language=en-us|others=Poetry Foundation|access-date=2018-07-21}}</ref> during that time.

Montfort and [[Georgia Institute of Technology]] professor [[Ian Bogost]] wrote ''[[Racing the Beam: The Atari Video Computer System]]'' (MIT Press, 2009), a study of world's first widespread gaming system, the [[Atari 2600]]. In the book, they analyze the platforms, or systems, that underlie the [[computing]] process. They also discuss the social and cultural implications of the system that dominated the [[video game]] market.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://archive.boston.com/bostonglobe/ideas/articles/2009/03/08/a_talk_with_nick_montfort/|title=A talk with Nick Montfort|last=Edgers|first=Geoff|date=March 8, 2009|work=The Boston Globe}}</ref>. Montfort along with nine other co-authors wrote ''10 PRINT CHR$(205.5+RND(1)); : GOTO 10'' (MIT Press, 2012), or simply ''10 PRINT'', a study of the titular [[One-liner program|one-line]] [[BASIC]] program for the [[Commodore 64]]. Using the program as a template, ''10 Print'' addresses the cultural phenomenon of computer programs, the randomness and regularity in computing and art and the maze in popular culture.<ref>{{cite web
 |title=10 PRINT CHR$(205.5)+RND(1); : GOTO 10
 |url=https://10print.org/
 |website=10 PRINT
 |access-date=17 July 2026
}}</ref>

His most recent book is ''The Future'' (MIT Press, 2017). A [[futures studies]] reviewer describes ''The Future'' as "written by an outsider to the foresight community" who "examines the works of artists, inventors, and designers and how they have imagined the future."<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://aaiforesight.com/blog/book-review-future|title=Book Review: The Future {{!}} AAI Foresight|website=aaiforesight.com|language=en|access-date=2018-07-21}}</ref> The book was reviewed as "striking a balance between planning and poetry ... a sober, tight account of what 'the future' is and has been, as well as how to think and make it."<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://itp.nyu.edu/adjacent/issue-3/a-review-of-the-future/|title=A Review of The Future|date=2018-06-05|work=ADJACENT Issue 3|access-date=2018-07-21|language=en-US}}</ref>
